title: Returning from paternity leave into an AI-driven company pivot
situation: When I returned to House Numbers after a long paternity leave, the engineering team consisted of three people and the company still operated with a B2C model. Two weeks later, our CEO told us that the model was not working and that the company would pivot to a B2B mortgage platform built heavily around AI. This was early in the LLM boom. We had run a few experiments, but none of us had a real background in machine learning, LLMs, or agents. I normally have a lot of confidence in my ability to learn and solve technical problems. This time I could not see it. I was exhausted, emotionally overwhelmed, and still adapting to becoming a father when the company changed both its business and its technical direction. The combination made the new work feel beyond me.
task: I seriously considered leaving because I did not want to slow down the team or become a burden while everyone else was trying to make the pivot work. I had to decide whether to stay and learn the new AI work or leave.
actions: Before making that decision, I spoke openly with my CTO, who told me that the rest of the team was probably facing the same technical uncertainty. A teammate then shared that he also felt a strong sense of impostor syndrome around the new AI work.

My wife and my colleagues could still see my ability clearly during a period when I could not. They listened and adjusted expectations. Some of the workload was shared, and I had space to recover while learning alongside them.

Once I started working directly with LLMs, the change in perspective came quickly. The names and tools were new, but the underlying work still involved problems I had handled throughout my career: system boundaries, data contracts, failure modes, testing, and operational tradeoffs. I already knew how to enter an unfamiliar technical domain and work out its rules. I had simply lost sight of that while exhausted.
results: Over the following years, I became one of the engineers building House Numbers' production LLM and agentic systems, with work ranging from the Communication Service to evaluation infrastructure and operational tooling.
Areas that had initially made me question my place became areas where teammates regularly trusted my judgment.
reflection: I keep coming back to this story because it reminds me what I am capable of. I entered the pivot convinced that I might become a burden, then helped build the production systems that made AI central to House Numbers' new direction. That result gives my confidence something concrete to rest on. I know I am very good at what I do, and I trust the depth of my engineering experience. When a new technical challenge arrives, I may need to learn its language and tools, but I know I have the skills to find a sound way through it once I decide to begin.
